blocks.text: 1. Brute Force Search
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447302305-582983981.png
Brute Force Search opens the ANN Search Algorithms module with the simplest possible baseline, moving the discussion from storage to the actual search algorithms.
It compares a query vector against every single stored vector, one by one, the simplest possible search method there is.
2. Vector Databases Recap
The eleven topics of the Vector Databases module built a durable, organized storage layer for vectors.
This module covers the actual search algorithms that run against that storage.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Module","Role"],"rows":[["Vector Databases","Provides durable, organized storage for vectors"],["ANN Search Algorithms","Provides the algorithms that search that storage"]]}

blocks.text: 3. The Simplest Possible Search
Brute force search checks every stored vector with no shortcuts at all, unlike the specialized indexes discussed in What is a Vector Database.
It is the most straightforward, and most mathematically exact, search method possible.
4. Guaranteed Correctness
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447302305-338872753.png
Checking every vector guarantees finding the true, mathematically closest match every time.
No approximation, shortcut, or index structure stands between the query and a perfect answer.
5. The Linear Scaling Problem
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447302554-141190518.png
Search time grows directly with the number of stored vectors, the same approximate-versus-exact tradeoff raised in What is a Vector Database.
Doubling the collection size doubles the time every single query takes.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A collection that grows from ten thousand to ten million vectors makes brute force search roughly a thousand times slower per query, a scaling problem that becomes untenable at real world sizes.

blocks.text: 6. Where Brute Force Remains Practical
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447302556-117494276.png
A small collection, from hundreds to a few thousand vectors, searches fast enough even without any index.
The overhead of building an index may not be worth it at that small scale.
7. Brute Force As A Ground Truth

blocks.alt: Brute Force As A Ground Truth
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447302556-546413147.png
Brute force results serve as the correct answer that approximate methods get measured against, the same role exact evaluation plays in Embedding Evaluation.
Every faster algorithm covered later in this module gets judged by how close it comes to this baseline.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Every approximate algorithm covered later in this module gets evaluated by comparing its results against brute force search's guaranteed correct answer, making brute force essential even when it is too slow to use directly in production.

blocks.text: 8. Hardware Parallelization
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447302557-967201636.png
Comparing vectors is a highly parallelizable operation, well suited to modern hardware.
Specialized hardware can push brute force search further than naive intuition might suggest.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Brute Force Search Remains The Right Choice

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Brute Force Search Remains The Right Choice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447302557-275652198.png
Small collections and correctness benchmarking suit brute force well.
Large, latency sensitive production collections need the approximate algorithms covered later in this module instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below runs brute force search and measures how its time scales with collection size.

code.content:
import time
import random

def euclidean_distance(v1, v2):
    return sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) ** 0.5

def brute_force_search(query, vectors, top_k=1):
    # checks every vector with no shortcuts
    distances = [(i, euclidean_distance(query, v)) for i, v in enumerate(vectors)]
    distances.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
    return distances[:top_k]

for size in [1_000, 5_000, 20_000]:
    vectors = [[random.random() for _ in range(64)] for _ in range(size)]
    query = [random.random() for _ in range(64)]

    start = time.time()
    results = brute_force_search(query, vectors, top_k=3)
    elapsed = time.time() - start

    print(f"Collection size {size:,}: {elapsed:.4f} seconds")

print("\nNotice search time grows roughly in proportion to collection size.")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows search time growing directly in proportion to collection size, the linear scaling problem that motivates every approximate algorithm covered across the rest of this module.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using brute force search on a very large collection where approximate methods would be far faster.
Never using brute force at all, even as a correctness benchmark for approximate algorithms.
Assuming brute force cannot benefit from parallel hardware acceleration.
Building an index for a tiny collection where brute force would have been simpler and fast enough.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Brute force search compares a query vector against every single stored vector, one by one.
It is the simplest and most mathematically exact search method available.
Checking every vector guarantees finding the true, mathematically closest match every time.
Search time grows directly with collection size, becoming impractical at large scale.
Small collections can search fast enough with brute force alone, without needing an index.
Brute force results serve as the ground truth that approximate methods are measured against.
Comparing vectors is highly parallelizable, letting specialized hardware extend brute force feasibility.
Large, latency sensitive production collections need the approximate algorithms covered later in this module.
